## Introduction

Tim Sainburg's 2025 paper includes a breadth of modern techniques and analysis used in the Gentner Lab, making it a useful paper to simulate in order to familiarize myself with relevant concepts and data. I will be simulating behavioral data from a two-alternative choice task (2AC) where the choices are modulated by the reliabilty of an auditory primer cue. My main analysis goal is to find a significant difference in the population psychometric curve inflection points for decision making based on the reliability of the primer cue. This simulation will engage my interest in sensory systems while allowing me to work with real data and get experience analyzing it. 

For this project, I will need to simulate a new data set, clean it to calculate the necessary analytic points (such as change in inflection point), create a linear mixed effects model, and create a 2 distribution histogram (figure 3e in the original paper). I will be aiming to replicate analysis with statistics similar to those reported in the paper (β = −11.12, s.e.m. = 1.158,
z = −9.6, P < 0.001) I believe that this will be an adequate challenge because it is a large dataset, and I do not have any experience with linear mixed effects models. I will need to ensure that I am cleaning and analyzing such a large dataset accurately and take the necessary steps to understand linear mixed effects models. Another challenge will be choosing simulation parameters that accuratley model the behavioral data. Although the data is not available in this paper, it is available in another paper (Gorman et al 2026) that analyzes the same dataset, making it easier to simulate an accurate representation of the data. 

Learning Goals: My main goal is to re-familiarize myself with data analysis in R. I have used the language a few times for smaller projects, but without consistent use, I stil do not feel confident in my programming abilities. Although I anticipate challenges due to my inexperience, my conceptual understanding of the data, paper, and general programming knowledge make the scope of this project feasible for me. I also want to use this project as an opportunity to gain a greater understanding of linear mixed effects models, what they can tell us, and how to use them.

## Methods

### Description of the steps required to reproduce the results

To reproduce the key result from this study, I will first need to change the data into a usable form. The pickle files need to be converted into files that R can use and stored in the repository instead of a local machine. I will need to create a data frame from these individual data files, and this data frame will benefit from being cleaned to remove extraneous variables. I will need to keep the "cue prob," "correct," "interpolation point," and other values that I will need to discuss with the author to reduce ambiguity. After cleaning, I will need to simulate new data based on the parameters of the real data. I will keep experimental values the same, and only change response values based on parameters observed in the original data. After simulating, I will make a new dataframe for the the dual histogram from figure 3e. This figure is strictly for interpretation purposes and does not have associated statistical tests. Axes in the paper are imprecise, so confirmation of replication will need to be done visually. Interpolation is defined as the degree of the model generated mixture of auditory stimuli based on the 128 syllable continuum. Next, I will make a data frame to recreate figure 3f, including probability of accurate cue and inflection value. This visualization includes individual trial data, averaged individual data, averaged population data, and standard population level error. I will need to design a pipeline to include these statistics. I will need to fit a trendline using a linear mixed effects model. The model tests psychometric inflection point changing as a result of the main effect of cue probability while accounting for random effects of subject and cue response per subject. I plan on calculating the same statistics from the linear mixed effects model that are reported in the paper: cue probability: β = −11.12, s.e.m. = 1.158, z = −9.6, P < 0.001. 

### Differences from original study

The original study runs these analyses and visualizations in Python, meaning that I will need to rebuild the code for it to fit into my analysis in R. I anticipate that this difference may change the appearance and aesthetics of my data visualizations, but I do not anticipate it significantly changing the statistical values returned. Running a simulation introduces structured variation, so I anticipate values in my figures and statistics to look slightly different, but not to an extent that alters the findings to a significant degree. The large effect size and the small p-value lead me to believe that simulating the data will not significantly change the statistical returns. 

## Project Progress Check 1

### Measure of success

I will measure success by comparing the simulated β to the original confidence interval. Additionally, I will analyze the extent to which a shift could occur if the bird was not influenced by the prior cue.  


### Pipeline progress

Earlier in this report, you described the steps necessary to reproduce the key result(s) of this study. Please describe your progress on each of these steps (e.g., data preprocessing, model fitting, model evaluation).

Right now, I have roughly recreated the 3 figures from the paper I am replicating. I am still working out some differences between the figures in the paper and my replications. I will also need to run a linear mixed effects model to replicate the reported effect size in the paper. After these steps, I will need to create a simulated dataset without the reported main effect to see the differences in the figures and statistics. There is still a lot of work to be done, but having a functioning data pipeline that recreates the targeted figures is a big step forward.

``` {r}

#### Load Relevant Libraries and Functions
library(here)
library(tidyverse)
library(lme4)
library(lmerTest)
library(assertthat)

```

```{r}
#cleaning for fig 3b

#| cache: true

#### Function that cleans one bird's raw file
clean_bird <- function(path) {
  bird_id <- sub("\\.csv(\\.gz)?$", "", basename(path))
  
  d <- read_csv(path, show_col_types = FALSE) |>
    filter(cueing) |>   # experimental phase only
    mutate(
      p_signal_right = case_when(
        cue_class == "NC"     ~ 0.5,          # no-cue condition
        cue_class == "CN"     ~ 0.5,          # uninformative cue
        cue_direction == "R"  ~ cue_prob,
        cue_direction == "L"  ~ 1 - cue_prob,
        TRUE                  ~ NA_real_      
      ),
      # P(reinforce left | cue)
      p_signal_left = round(1 - p_signal_right, 3),
      bird = bird_id
    ) |>
    filter(!is.na(p_signal_left), !is.na(response_bool))
  
  # Put every morph in the same orientation (flip any morph that falls)
  x_min  <- min(d$interpolation_point)
  x_max  <- max(d$interpolation_point)
  x_span <- x_max - x_min
  
  morph_direction <- d |>
    group_by(interpolation) |>
    summarise(
      low_end  = mean(response_bool[interpolation_point <= x_min + x_span * 0.25]),
      high_end = mean(response_bool[interpolation_point >= x_max - x_span * 0.25]),
      .groups = "drop"
    ) |>
    mutate(flip = low_end > high_end)
  
  d |>
    left_join(select(morph_direction, interpolation, flip), by = "interpolation") |>
    mutate(
      interpolation_point = if_else(flip, x_min + x_max - interpolation_point,
                                    interpolation_point),
      n_flipped_morphs = sum(morph_direction$flip)
    ) |>
    # keep only what the plot needs, so column types match across birds
    select(bird, interpolation, interpolation_point, cue_class, cue_prob,
           cue_direction, p_signal_left, response_bool, n_flipped_morphs)
}

#### clean all raw files
raw_files <- list.files(here("data"), pattern = "^B\\d+\\.csv(\\.gz)?$", full.names = TRUE)

df_all <- map(raw_files, clean_bird, .progress = TRUE) |>
  list_rbind()

dir.create(here("data", "clean"), showWarnings = FALSE)
write_csv(df_all, here("data", "clean", "all_birds_clean.csv.gz"))
```

``` {r}
# plotting fig 3b

#### proportion of right pecks per bird, cue condition, and point
plot_data <- df_all |>
  group_by(bird, p_signal_left, interpolation_point) |>
  summarise(
    p_right  = mean(response_bool),
    n_trials = n(),
    .groups  = "drop"
  )

#### panel order
bird_order <- c("B1174","B1426","B1170","B1432","B1437",
                "B1433","B1597","B1427","B1188","B1244",
                "B1590","B1399","B1591","B1252","B1110",
                "B1390","B1248","B1593","B1595","B1276")

plot_data <- plot_data |> mutate(bird = factor(bird, levels = bird_order))

#### logistic fit, one fit per bird x cue
fit_logistic <- function(d) {
  nls(
    p_right ~ p_max + (p_min - p_max) / (1 + (interpolation_point / inflection)^slope),
    data = d,
    weights = n_trials,
    start = list(p_min = 0.1, p_max = 0.9, inflection = 64, slope = 10),
    algorithm = "port",
    lower = c(p_min = 0,   p_max = 0.5, inflection = 1,   slope = 0.1),
    upper = c(p_min = 0.5, p_max = 1,   inflection = 128, slope = 100)
  )
}

fits <- plot_data |>
  group_by(bird, p_signal_left) |>
  nest() |>
  mutate(model = map(data, possibly(fit_logistic, otherwise = NULL)))

# Which fits failed to converge?
fits |>
  filter(map_lgl(model, is.null)) |>
  select(bird, p_signal_left) |>
  print(n = Inf)

#### Predicted curves
x_grid <- seq(min(plot_data$interpolation_point),
              max(plot_data$interpolation_point),
              length.out = 200)

curve_data <- fits |>
  filter(!map_lgl(model, is.null)) |>
  mutate(pred = map(model, \(m) tibble(
    interpolation_point = x_grid,
    p_right = predict(m, newdata = tibble(interpolation_point = x_grid))
  ))) |>
  select(bird, p_signal_left, pred) |>
  unnest(pred)

#### colors
cue_colors <- c("0.125" = "#7b1e4a", "0.25" = "#c0447f", "0.5" = "gray40",
                "0.75" = "#6a5acd", "0.875" = "#2b2a73")

#### plot
ggplot(plot_data, aes(x = interpolation_point, y = p_right,
                           color = factor(p_signal_left))) +
  geom_point(size = 0.6, alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_line(data = curve_data, linewidth = 0.6) +
  facet_wrap(~ bird, ncol = 5) +
  scale_color_manual(values = cue_colors) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1), breaks = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(x = "Syllable continuum (interpolation point)",
       y = "P(peck right)",
       color = "P(reinforce left | cue)") +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(strip.background = element_blank(),
        strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"))

```

``` {r}
# fig 3e cleaning

df_all <- read_csv(here("data", "clean", "all_birds_clean.csv.gz"), show_col_types = FALSE)

#### Keep the two strongest cues, informative trials only (L or R direction)
cued <- df_all |>
  filter(cue_prob %in% c(0.75, 0.875), cue_direction %in% c("L", "R"))

#### Proportion of right pecks per bird, morph, cue strength, cue direction, and point
# Assumes the `interpolation` column identifies the morph
cue_summary <- cued |>
  group_by(bird, interpolation, cue_prob, cue_direction, interpolation_point) |>
  summarise(
    p_right  = mean(response_bool),
    n_trials = n(),
    .groups  = "drop"
  )

#### Four-parameter logistic
fit_logistic <- function(d) {
  nls(
    p_right ~ p_max + (p_min - p_max) / (1 + (interpolation_point / inflection)^slope),
    data = d,
    weights = n_trials,
    start = list(p_min = 0.1, p_max = 0.9, inflection = 64, slope = 10),
    algorithm = "port",
    lower = c(p_min = 0,   p_max = 0.5, inflection = 1,   slope = 0.1),
    upper = c(p_min = 0.5, p_max = 1,   inflection = 128, slope = 100)
  )
}

#### One fit per bird x morph x cue strength x cue direction
fits <- cue_summary |>
  group_by(bird, interpolation, cue_prob, cue_direction) |>
  nest() |>
  mutate(
    model = map(data, \(d) suppressWarnings(possibly(fit_logistic, otherwise = NULL)(d))),
    inflection = map_dbl(model, \(m) if (is.null(m)) NA_real_ else coef(m)[["inflection"]])
  ) |>
  ungroup()

#### Fit quality: how many failed or landed on a bound?
fits |>
  summarise(
    n_fits     = n(),
    n_failed   = sum(is.na(inflection)),
    n_at_bound = sum(inflection <= 1.5 | inflection >= 127.5, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |>
  print()

#### ΔInflection = left-cue inflection minus right-cue inflection
delta <- fits |>
  filter(!is.na(inflection), inflection > 1.5, inflection < 127.5) |>   # drop failed / at-bound fits
  select(bird, interpolation, cue_prob, cue_direction, inflection) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = cue_direction, values_from = inflection) |>
  drop_na(L, R) |>
  mutate(delta_inflection = L - R)

#### Checks
delta |> count(cue_prob)  
delta |>
  group_by(cue_prob) |>
  summarise(mean_delta = mean(delta_inflection),
            sd_delta   = sd(delta_inflection))   # means should be POSITIVE

write_csv(delta, here("data", "clean", "delta_inflection.csv"))
```

```{r}

### Simulation setup

set.seed(2026)

#### Real trial structure, collapsed to one row per cell
df_all <- read_csv(here("data", "clean", "all_birds_clean.csv.gz"), show_col_types = FALSE)

cells <- df_all |>
  group_by(bird, interpolation, cue_class, p_signal_left, interpolation_point) |>
  summarise(n_trials = n(), k_real = sum(response_bool), .groups = "drop")

#### Four-parameter logistic
logistic4 <- function(x, p_min, p_max, inflection, slope) {
  p_max + (p_min - p_max) / (1 + (x / inflection)^slope)
}

# same fit as 3b/3e/3f
fit_logistic <- function(d) {
  nls(
    p_right ~ p_max + (p_min - p_max) / (1 + (interpolation_point / inflection)^slope),
    data = d,
    weights = n_trials,
    start = list(p_min = 0.1, p_max = 0.9, inflection = 64, slope = 10),
    algorithm = "port",
    lower = c(p_min = 0,   p_max = 0.5, inflection = 1,   slope = 0.1),
    upper = c(p_min = 0.5, p_max = 1,   inflection = 128, slope = 100)
  )
}

#### Baseline curve for each bird x morph, fit to the real no-cue (NC) trials
nc_fits <- cells |>
  filter(cue_class == "NC") |>
  mutate(p_right = k_real / n_trials) |>
  group_by(bird, interpolation) |>
  nest() |>
  mutate(par = map(data, \(d) {
    m <- suppressWarnings(possibly(fit_logistic, otherwise = NULL)(d))
    if (is.null(m)) {
      tibble(p_min = NA_real_, p_max = NA_real_, base_infl = NA_real_, slope = NA_real_)
    } else {
      as_tibble_row(coef(m)) |> rename(base_infl = inflection)
    }
  })) |>
  ungroup() |>
  select(-data) |>
  unnest(par)

sum(is.na(nc_fits$base_infl))   # how many baseline fits failed

# failed fits borrow the median of the successful ones
morph_pars <- nc_fits |>
  mutate(across(c(p_min, p_max, base_infl, slope),
                \(x) if_else(is.na(x), median(x, na.rm = TRUE), x)))

#### Truth: start from the real LMM (in terms of p_signal_left, centered at 0.5)
real_fits <- read_csv(here("data", "clean", "inflection_by_cue.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(pl_c = p_signal_left - 0.5)

m_real <- lmer(inflection ~ pl_c + (1 + pl_c | bird), data = real_fits)
beta_true <- fixef(m_real)[["pl_c"]]                           # positive, about +11.8
sd_u_true <- attr(VarCorr(m_real)$bird, "stddev")[["pl_c"]]    # bird-level SD of the shift
sd_u_sim  <- sd_u_true * 1.25    # tuning factor; adjust after each trial run
c(beta_true = beta_true, sd_u_true = sd_u_true)
# can overwrite these^ with round numbers to test a specific scenario

#### Simulator: keeps the real trial counts, replaces only the responses
simulate_cells <- function(cells, morph_pars, beta, sd_u) {
  birds <- tibble(bird = unique(cells$bird)) |>
    mutate(u_bird = rnorm(n(), 0, sd_u))        # new bird-level shift deviations each call

  cells |>
    left_join(birds, by = "bird") |>
    left_join(morph_pars, by = c("bird", "interpolation")) |>
    mutate(
      infl = pmin(pmax(base_infl + (beta + u_bird) * (p_signal_left - 0.5), 1), 128),
      p    = logistic4(interpolation_point, p_min, p_max, infl, slope),
      k    = rbinom(n(), n_trials, p)
    ) |>
    select(bird, interpolation, cue_class, p_signal_left,
           interpolation_point, n_trials, k)
}

```

``` {r}

### Recover parameters from simulated cells

#| cache: true

recover_effect <- function(cells_k) {          
  fits <- cells_k |>
    mutate(p_right = k / n_trials) |>
    group_by(bird, interpolation, cue_class, p_signal_left) |>
    nest() |>
    mutate(
      model = map(data, \(d) suppressWarnings(possibly(fit_logistic, otherwise = NULL)(d))),
      inflection = map_dbl(model, \(m) if (is.null(m)) NA_real_ else coef(m)[["inflection"]])
    ) |>
    ungroup()

  good <- fits |>
    filter(!is.na(inflection), inflection > 1.5, inflection < 127.5) |>
    mutate(pl_c = p_signal_left - 0.5)

  m <- tryCatch(
    suppressMessages(suppressWarnings(
      lmer(inflection ~ pl_c + (1 + pl_c | bird), data = good))),
    error = \(e) NULL)

  tibble(
    n_fits        = nrow(fits),
    n_failed      = sum(is.na(fits$inflection)),
    n_kept        = nrow(good),
    sd_inflection = sd(good$inflection),
    r2            = cor(good$p_signal_left, good$inflection)^2,
    beta_hat      = if (is.null(m)) NA_real_ else fixef(m)[["pl_c"]],
    se            = if (is.null(m)) NA_real_ else coef(summary(m))["pl_c", "Std. Error"],
    sd_u_hat      = if (is.null(m)) NA_real_ else attr(VarCorr(m)$bird, "stddev")[["pl_c"]],
    p_value       = if (is.null(m)) NA_real_ else coef(summary(m))["pl_c", "Pr(>|t|)"],
    singular      = if (is.null(m)) NA else isSingular(m)
  )
}

#### Calibration: real data vs. one simulated dataset through the identical pipeline
real_check <- recover_effect(mutate(cells, k = k_real))
one_sim    <- recover_effect(simulate_cells(cells, morph_pars, beta_true, sd_u_sim))

bind_rows(real = real_check, simulated = one_sim, .id = "data")
# Compare sd_inflection, r2, n_failed / n_fits, and sd_u_hat.
# Adjust the generating parameters (see notes) until these agree.

#### Many replicates
n_sims <- 200

sims <- map(seq_len(n_sims),
            \(i) recover_effect(simulate_cells(cells, morph_pars, beta_true, sd_u_sim)),
            .progress = TRUE) |>
  list_rbind() |>
  mutate(sim = row_number())

sims |>
  summarise(
    mean_beta_hat = mean(beta_hat, na.rm = TRUE),
    bias          = mean(beta_hat - beta_true, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd_beta_hat   = sd(beta_hat, na.rm = TRUE),
    coverage      = mean(abs(beta_hat - beta_true) < 1.96 * se, na.rm = TRUE),
    mean_sd_u_hat = mean(sd_u_hat, na.rm = TRUE),
    pct_singular  = mean(singular, na.rm = TRUE),
    pct_failed    = mean(n_failed / n_fits)
  )

write_csv(sims, here("data", "clean", "simulation_results_sd_u_1.25.csv"))

```

```{r}
set.seed(2027)

sims_null <- map(seq_len(n_sims),

    mean_se        = mean(se, na.rm = TRUE),                        # should be close to sd_beta_hat
    false_pos_rate = mean(p_value < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE),            # should be near 0.05
    mean_sd_u_hat  = mean(sd_u_hat, na.rm = TRUE),
    pct_singular   = mean(singular, na.rm = TRUE),
    pct_failed     = mean(n_failed / n_fits)
  )
```

``` {r}
#cleaning for 3-panel 3f comparison

#### Returns the kept morph-level fits (same filters as 3f) for one dataset
recover_fits <- function(cells_k) {          # needs columns n_trials and k
  cells_k |>
    mutate(p_right = k / n_trials) |>
    group_by(bird, interpolation, cue_class, p_signal_left) |>
    nest() |>
    mutate(
      model = map(data, \(d) suppressWarnings(possibly(fit_logistic, otherwise = NULL)(d))),
      inflection = map_dbl(model, \(m) if (is.null(m)) NA_real_ else coef(m)[["inflection"]])
    ) |>
    ungroup() |>
    filter(!is.na(inflection), inflection > 1.5, inflection < 127.5) |>
    select(bird, interpolation, cue_class, p_signal_left, inflection)
}

#### Real data (saved at the end of the 3f cleaning chunk)
real_fits <- read_csv(here("data", "clean", "inflection_by_cue.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  select(bird, interpolation, cue_class, p_signal_left, inflection)

#### One simulated dataset with the real effect, one with the null
set.seed(2028)
sim_effect_fits <- recover_fits(simulate_cells(cells, morph_pars, beta_true, sd_u_sim))
sim_null_fits   <- recover_fits(simulate_cells(cells, morph_pars, beta = 0, sd_u = sd_u_sim))

#### Checks: all three should be close to 1,050 fits
c(real = nrow(real_fits), effect = nrow(sim_effect_fits), null = nrow(sim_null_fits))

write_csv(sim_effect_fits, here("data", "clean", "sim_effect_fits.csv"))
write_csv(sim_null_fits,   here("data", "clean", "sim_null_fits.csv"))

```

```{r}
#plotting for 3-panel fig 3f comparison

### Figure 3f: real data vs. simulated effect vs. simulated null

#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 9

#### Stack the three datasets, with panel labels
panel_levels <- c("Real data", "Simulated: real effect", "Simulated: null effect")

all_fits <- bind_rows(
  "Real data"              = real_fits,
  "Simulated: real effect" = sim_effect_fits,
  "Simulated: null effect" = sim_null_fits,
  .id = "dataset"
) |>
  mutate(dataset = factor(dataset, levels = panel_levels))

### Assertthat sanity checks before plotting
#### 1. Structure: required columns and the three expected datasets
assert_that(
  has_name(all_fits, c("dataset", "bird", "interpolation", "cue_class",
                       "p_signal_left", "inflection")),
  msg = "all_fits is missing one of the required columns"
)

expected_panels <- c("Real data", "Simulated: real effect", "Simulated: null effect")
assert_that(
  setequal(levels(all_fits$dataset), expected_panels),
  msg = "dataset should have exactly the three panel labels"
)

#### 2. Values: no missing inflections, all inside the range nls was allowed to return
assert_that(
  noNA(all_fits$inflection),
  msg = "There are NA inflection values; failed fits should have been dropped"
)
assert_that(
  all(all_fits$inflection > 1.5 & all_fits$inflection < 127.5),
  msg = "Some inflections sit at the nls bounds; they should have been filtered out"
)

#### 3. Cue coding: only the five expected P(reinforce left) values
assert_that(
  all(round(all_fits$p_signal_left, 3) %in% c(0.125, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 0.875)),
  msg = "Unexpected p_signal_left values found"
)

#### 4. Sample size: each panel should be close to the paper's n = 1,050
counts <- all_fits |> count(dataset)
print(counts)
assert_that(
  all(counts$n >= 1000 & counts$n <= 1050),
  msg = "A panel has fewer than 1,000 or more than 1,050 fits; check failed fits and CN handling"
)

#### 5. Coverage: all 20 birds in every panel, and no duplicated fits
birds_per_panel <- all_fits |> group_by(dataset) |> summarise(n_birds = n_distinct(bird))
assert_that(
  all(birds_per_panel$n_birds == 20),
  msg = "A panel does not contain all 20 birds"
)

dupes <- all_fits |> count(dataset, bird, interpolation, cue_class, p_signal_left) |> filter(n > 1)
assert_that(
  nrow(dupes) == 0,
  msg = "Duplicate bird x morph x cue-condition fits found"
)

#### 6. Direction of the effect (the sign check we used throughout)
slopes <- all_fits |>
  group_by(dataset) |>
  summarise(fit = list(lm(inflection ~ p_signal_left)), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(slope = map_dbl(fit, \(m) coef(m)[["p_signal_left"]]),
         se    = map_dbl(fit, \(m) coef(summary(m))["p_signal_left", "Std. Error"]))
print(slopes |> select(dataset, slope, se))

slope_of <- function(panel) slopes$slope[slopes$dataset == panel]
se_of    <- function(panel) slopes$se[slopes$dataset == panel]

# These two are deterministic expectations: they should always be clearly positive
assert_that(slope_of("Real data") > 0,
            msg = "Real data slope is not positive: check orientation / L-R coding")
assert_that(slope_of("Simulated: real effect") > 0,
            msg = "Simulated-effect slope is not positive")

# The null check is statistical, so one random draw can wander. Warn instead of stopping.
null_ok <- see_if(
  abs(slope_of("Simulated: null effect")) < 3 * se_of("Simulated: null effect"),
  msg = "Null-panel slope is more than 3 SE from zero; check for a bug, or try another seed"
)
if (!null_ok) warning(attr(null_ok, "msg"))

message("All 3f data checks passed")

#### Colors: maroon -> blue like the paper, gray for the 0.5 conditions
cue_colors <- c("0.125" = "#7b1e4a", "0.25" = "#c0447f", "0.5" = "gray40",
                "0.75" = "#6a5acd", "0.875" = "#2b2a73")

#### Bird-level means (colored triangles), per panel
bird_means <- all_fits |>
  group_by(dataset, bird, p_signal_left) |>
  summarise(inflection = mean(inflection), .groups = "drop")

#### Across-bird means with s.e.m. (black triangles and error bars), per panel
cue_means <- bird_means |>
  group_by(dataset, p_signal_left) |>
  summarise(
    mean_inflection = mean(inflection),
    sem = sd(inflection) / sqrt(n()),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

#### r² and P for each panel (Pearson, over all morph-level fits)
stat_labels <- all_fits |>
  group_by(dataset) |>
  summarise(ct = list(cor.test(p_signal_left, inflection)), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(label = map_chr(ct, \(x) paste0("r² = ", sprintf("%.3f", x$estimate^2),
                                         "\nP = ", format.pval(x$p.value, digits = 2))))

#### Plot
p <- ggplot() +
  geom_jitter(data = all_fits,
              aes(x = p_signal_left, y = inflection, color = factor(p_signal_left)),
              width = 0.02, height = 0, size = 1, alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_point(data = bird_means,
             aes(x = p_signal_left, y = inflection, color = factor(p_signal_left)),
             shape = 17, size = 2, alpha = 0.8,
             position = position_jitter(width = 0.02, height = 0)) +
  geom_smooth(data = all_fits,
              aes(x = p_signal_left, y = inflection),
              method = "lm", se = FALSE,
              color = "black", linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_errorbar(data = cue_means,
                aes(x = p_signal_left,
                    ymin = mean_inflection - sem, ymax = mean_inflection + sem),
                width = 0.03, color = "black") +
  geom_point(data = cue_means,
             aes(x = p_signal_left, y = mean_inflection),
             shape = 17, size = 3, color = "black") +
  geom_text(data = stat_labels,
            aes(x = 0.08, y = Inf, label = label),
            hjust = 0, vjust = 1.3, size = 3.5, inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~ dataset, ncol = 1) +
  scale_color_manual(values = cue_colors, guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8)) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0.05, 0.95)) +
  labs(x = "P(reinforce left | cue)", y = "Inflection") +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(strip.background = element_blank(),
        strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"))

print(p)
```

```{r}
#cleaning for 3-panel 3e comparison

#### Read the saved morph-level fits (the same ones used for the 3f comparison)
read_fits <- function(file) {
  read_csv(here("data", "clean", file), show_col_types = FALSE) |>
    select(bird, interpolation, cue_class, p_signal_left, inflection)
}

all_fits <- bind_rows(
  "Real data"              = read_fits("inflection_by_cue.csv"),
  "Simulated: real effect" = read_fits("sim_effect_fits.csv"),
  "Simulated: null effect" = read_fits("sim_null_fits.csv"),
  .id = "dataset"
) |>
  mutate(dataset = factor(dataset, levels = c("Real data", "Simulated: real effect",
                                              "Simulated: null effect")))

#### Keep the informative cues (CL = left cue, CR = right cue) at 0.75 and 0.875
# p_signal_left is the P(reinforce left), so for a right cue the cue strength is 1 - p_signal_left
delta <- all_fits |>
  filter(cue_class %in% c("CL", "CR")) |>
  mutate(cue_prob = round(if_else(cue_class == "CL", p_signal_left, 1 - p_signal_left), 3)) |>
  filter(cue_prob %in% c(0.75, 0.875)) |>
  select(dataset, bird, interpolation, cue_prob, cue_class, inflection) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = cue_class, values_from = inflection) |>
  drop_na(CL, CR) |>
  mutate(delta_inflection = CL - CR)    # left-cue minus right-cue, as in the 3e code

#### Checks
delta |> count(dataset, cue_prob)    # the real data should be near your earlier counts
delta |>
  group_by(dataset, cue_prob) |>
  summarise(mean_delta = mean(delta_inflection),
            sd_delta   = sd(delta_inflection),
            .groups = "drop")
# real and simulated-effect means should be positive; the null means should be near 0

```

## Discussion

## Questions for 11/17 deadline
What assumptions does your generative model make about participant behavior, and which aspects of the real experiment does it simplify or omit?

The biggest assumption my generative model makes is that there is variation in bird level behavior similar to the variation from the original sample size. Although this experiment has a lot of data points from a lot of trials, 20 birds still isn't a lot. There could feasibly be a different spread of variation in behavior with even just a few birds behaving differently, leading to different parameters in the simulation, but this simulation only assumes the variation present in the experimental sample. The variation is also all bound in the sd_u value which is SD of the inflection shift. In the 3b plot, the logistic curve has parameters other than inflection point that also shift (intercepts, slope), but the simulation only changes the response based on inflection point shift. 

Identify one insight your simulation gave you about the strengths or limitations of the original experimental design.

Working with the data gave me a greater appreciation for the passive data collection aspect of the experimental design. In the past, I have had to run time intensive behavioral trials where I needed to be in the room to facilitate trials, but that wouldn't be feasible for a dataset of this size. A real strength of this design is the vast quantities of behavioral data that can be generated when a behavioral apparatus is set up to run trials without the presence of a researcher. This collection process that generates so much data allows for strong conclusions to be drawn about the experimental factors that influence behavior due to large sample sizes and trends across birds. 

Remaining steps: simulate another dataset absent of the main effect for comparison, plot this null dataset for easy comparison
